i
ABSTRACT
Objective: This article's primary purpose is to systematically review the literature on
whether portableandaffordable inertial sensors can reveal reliableinter-limb kinematic
asymmetries in ACL reconstructed (ACLR) patients.
Design: Systematic review following PRISMA-DTA guidelines
Methods: We conducted a database search of PUBMED, CINAHL, SCOPUS, and
SPORTDISCUS, checking for publications that compared the use of inertial sensors to
motion analysis systems, assessing subjects with ACLR during a dynamic test or
walking. The reviewers appraised every eligible study for its methodological quality
according to the QUADAS-2 checklist.
Results: Initially, 279 articles were retrievedand finally, fivemet theinclusion criteria.
In four studies, the extracted features from inertial sensors revealed significant inter-
limb differences in ACLR patients. Some of these features were strongly correlated
with metrics acquired from the motion analysis systems.
Conclusion: Inertial sensors can provide comparable information to motion analysis
systems during dynamic knee assessment after ACLR surgery. This has significant
potential for clinical use, enhancing patients' functional assessment and the monitoring
of the rehabilitation process.
Key words: inertial sensors, knee assessment, ACL, diagnostic accuracy

1. INTRODUCTION
Human motion analysis has a significant value in medicine, especially in orthopedics and
sports medicine. The measurement of movement and how the forces are applied during a
functional task can be valuable for appraising various surgical or therapeutic treatments (An,
1984).
Thestudy ofhumanmovement hasbecomeanareaof interest sincetheearliest times. During
the renaissance, the concurrent evolution of science and mathematics settled the foundations
for experimental observation. The unprecedented evolution of computer technology has
provided us with sophisticated systems to capture human motion (Colyer et al., 2018). The
gold standard for this purpose is a system consisting of cameras and retroreflective markers
attached to the human body's anatomical landmarks, providing 3D visualization (Baker et
al., 2007). Moreover, force measurement platformsin the ground provide the reaction forces
during motion, andthroughinverse dynamics, cancalculate net joint torques (Aurbach et al.,
2017). Lastly, EMG recordings produce accurate signals of electrical muscle activity (Raez
et al., 2006).
1.1 Optical motion capture systems
The term motion capture includes many systems for quantitatively recording body
movements. They can be divided into two major categories, optical and non-optical (Roggio
et al., 2021). The first category is camera-based systems. These derive motion data from
video recordings with special cameras. In the marker-based motion detection systems,
multiple markers, active (luminous) or passive (reflective), are placed on the subject's
prespecified anatomical landmarks according to various anthropometricmodels and adigital
3D representation is acquired. Then the video is captured from multiple angles using
multiple cameras. The markers' positions define the body's segments coordinates in space
and through mathematical algorithms and geometrical equations, the kinematics variables
for the joints of interest are calculated in all movement planes (frontal, sagittal, and
transversal). This is the most flexible and standard method used in the industry (Oppelt et
al., 2019).

--- PAGE 11 ---
2
A markerless motion detection system has also been developed. There is no need to mark
the body here. The software can track the subject's characteristics and infer relative motion
from the video. Those movement data can be mapped to existing frameworks such as 3D
models of the human body, hands, and face. Markerless systems can be based on regular
video cameras, but it is also common to use depth-sensitive cameras. Such cameras use
patterns of near-infrared light to recognize depth.
However, although these are still the gold-standard systems, they also have considerable
disadvantages; establishing a gait laboratory requires equipment purchases that average
$300,000 maintenance contracts for hardware and software ($30–$50,000) and full-time
laboratory personnel. Theyarealso time-consuming and confinedto a small collectionspace
(Simon et al., 2004).
1.2 Non optical motion capture systems
The second category, sensor-based systems, gets more detailed motion data from a small
number of specific points (Andriacchi et al., 2006). Lately, new technology acquired from
aerospace, industrial and robotic engineering appears a promising development in the field
of human motion analysis. Small, low-powered electromechanical sensors may bridge the
gap between large laboratory systems and clinical systems (Cuesta-Vargas et al., 2010).
These Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) use accelerometers, magnetometers,
and gyroscopes. Linear acceleration sensors are exclusively able to measure the acceleration
along a specific direction. These transducers can be classified into one- two- and three-axis
accelerometers depending on the number of sensitivity directions. When information
regarding the device's rotation in space is required, as in gait analysis, angular velocity
sensors (gyroscopes) must be added. A magnetometer measuring the earth's magnetic field
orientation is often added to the sensor assembly to allow for easier re-calibration of the
device and compensate for gyroscope drift issues. A device of a three-axis gyroscope and a
three-axis accelerometer is called an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). When a
magnetometer is also used, the device is known as MIMU (Magnetic Inertial Measurement
Unit) (Petraglia et al., 2019).

--- PAGE 12 ---
3
Worn on thebody segments, they providemotioninformationmeasured directlyonthebody,
and they can be used for in-field measurements. Sensors are usually placed on each recorded
body segment to derive joint kinematics. Rather than requiring accurate positioning, the user
calibrates the IMUs according to the segment's coordinate system. Therefore, the placement
procedure is less time-consuming compared to an optical system and their use requires much
less expertise (Bleser et al., 2017).
Figure 1.1: Types of motion capture systems
Numerous studies have incorporated IMUs for assessing gait, functional movements, and
sports activities throughout the literature. Gait analysis is the most commonly evaluated
activity (Weygers et al., 2020). Compared with an optical motion capture system, wearable
sensors can detect clinically relevant parameters with excellent test-retest reliability for all
spatio-temporal metrics (Teufl, 2019; Washabough, 2017; Cho, 2018). 3D joint kinematics
during dynamic tasks can also be assessed with a range of motion error below 3o
(Teufl et
al., 2019).
There is also an electromagnetic tracking system consisting of a transmitter and a sensor.
The transmitter emits a low-frequency magnetic field, and a sensor placed on the moving
motion capturesystems
optical
with markers
passive active
markerless
non optical
inertial magnetic electromagnetic

4
object measures the strength of each of these magnetic fields. From the field strength data
for each axis, you can calculatethepositionandorientation of thesensor (Stelzeret al,2004).
1.3 Anterior Cruciate Ligament
Muscles, ligaments, and menisci supply the knee joint with rigidity and stability, allowing it
to transfer enormous loads while performing numerous everyday duties (Markolf et al.,
1976). The anterior cruciate ligament is the primary static stabilizer against the anterior
translation of the tibia on the femur (Woo et al., 2006). It plays a vital role as a guide of the
screw-home mechanism of the knee. The tibia internally rotates when the knee flexes and
externally rotates as the femoral condyles roll and glide on the tibial plateau as the knee
extends—the knee joint locks in a position of maximum stability during full extension
(close-packed position) (Moglo et al., 2005).
For activeindividualswith an ACLrupture, ligament repair isthecurrent standardoftherapy
(Marx et al.,2003). When designing a personalized post-surgical rehabilitation protocol for
patients with ACLR, numerous factors should be considered, including the required return
activity level, time to surgical intervention, type of surgery and graft choice, post-surgical
muscle strength, and proprioceptive deficits (Della Villa et al., 2015). Despite the high
functional outcomes after reconstructive surgery, biomechanical abnormalities and
movement asymmetries can linger (Dunn et al., 2010). Biomechanical and neuromuscular
control deficits and imbalances are closely connected to secondary injury (Patterno et al.,
2010).
1.4 Biomechanical Asymmetries after ACLR
Several biomechanical studies examined the kinematic and kinetic characteristics of ACLR
patients. The ACLR groups had lower peak knee flexion angles, external knee flexion
moments, and external knee adduction moments during walking (Kaur et al., 2016). This
movement pattern during the loading phase of walking has been associated with cartilage
deterioration in the knee and may have a role in the progression of osteoarthritis following
ACLR (Slater et al., 2017).
Tibial rotation was observed to be substantially bigger in the ACLR knee compared to the
contralateral intact leg and the healthy control group in a subsequent examination with a
higher demand activity (stair descent and pivoting) (Ristanis et al., 2003). When combining

--- PAGE 14 ---
5
evidence, the most altered variables after ACLR are knee flexion motion and internal knee
extension moment, which are consistently smaller in the reconstructed limb while running
(Pairot-de-Fontenay et al., 2019).
Asymmetry was found more frequently in kinetic variables than in kinematic variables. The
asymmetry between limbs for peak vertical ground reaction force, peak knee-extension
moment, and loading rate during double-limb landings, as well as the mean knee-extension
moment and knee energy absorption during both double- and single-limb landings, appeared
to besignificantlyaffectedbyanteriorcruciateligamentreconstruction(Hugheset al., 2020).
1.5 Quadriceps Strength Deficits
Following ACL rupture and surgery, significant quadriceps atrophy progresses rapidly
(Williams et al., 2005). Strength impairments ranging from 2% to 20% have been
documented in participants more than two years after ACL surgery (Palmieri-Smith et al.,
2008). The underlying causes for such weakness are still unknown. Researchers have also
proposed that the inability to engage the quadriceps muscle fully (i.e., voluntary activation
failure) is a crucial source of persistent quadriceps weakness in persons who have had ACL
repair (Hart et al., 2010). This concept, however, has not been validated. Graft-related
muscular impairments occur following ACL repair. A patellar tendon transplant is related to
extensor deficits, whereas hamstring grafts are associated with flexion abnormalities
(Petersen et al., 2014). One of the most crucial rehabilitation goals following ACLR is to
restore lower extremity muscular strength (Buckthorpe et al., 2019).
Regarding the lower limb, knee osteoarthritis and total knee arthroplasty have been the two
most common musculoskeletal issues where inertial sensors are used as a diagnostic tool for
measuring risk factors and recovery.
1.6 Objectives
Thisarticle'sprimary purposeisto systematicallyreviewthe literatureontheinertial sensors'
use for functional assessment of patients who have undergone ACL reconstructive surgery.
To investigate whether IMUs can distinguish asymmetries in the function of the
reconstructed knee and whether metrics derived from IMUs can significantly correlate with
metrics from the gold standard motion analysis systems.

--- PAGE 15 ---
6
2. METHODS
This systematic review is based on Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and
Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Extension for Diagnostic Test Accuracy for reporting.
2.1Informationsourcesandsearchstrategy
We conducted systematic research in the following electronic databases: PubMed, Scopus,
Cinahl, Sportdiscus. The Boolean strategy is depicted in the table (2.1). Moreover, we
examined reference lists to retrieve relevant studies.
2.2 Study selection
The articles were initially imported into Endnote, and after removing duplicates, they were
screened by title and abstract. Two authors independently extracted data from the studies
according to the inclusion criteria.
2.3 Eligibility criteria
For the analysis, we included any study or trial that uses inertial sensor units to evaluate the
knee function during physical activities or special tests regarding the lower limp as long as
they are referred to a population undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstructive
surgery (ACLR). Thisanalysiscould beconductedin aclinical setting orahumanmovement
analysis lab but with the concurrent use of a gold standard motion analysis system. A
summary of inclusion and exclusion criteria is given in table 2.2
Table 2.1. Boolean search strategy
Database Keywords PubMed, Scopus, Cinahl, Sportdiscus
((inertial sensors) OR (IMUs)) AND ((anterior cruciate ligament) OR (ACL)) AND (deficits)
((inertial sensors) OR (IMUs)) AND ((anterior cruciate ligament) OR (ACL)) AND (assessment)
((inertial sensors) OR (IMUs)) AND ((anterior cruciate ligament) OR (ACL)) AND (injury)
((inertial sensors) OR (IMUs)) AND ((anterior cruciate ligament) OR (ACL)) AND (evaluation)
((inertial sensors) OR (IMUs)) AND ((anterior cruciate ligament) OR (ACL)) AND (asymmetries)
(accelerometry OR accelerometer OR gyroscope OR inertial sensor OR inertial measurement unit OR
wearable sensor OR wearable system OR wearable device OR IMU OR MEMS) AND (anterior cruciate
ligament OR ACL)

2.4 Assessment of risk of bias
The retrieved documents were assessed for methodological quality using the QUADAS-2
checklist in four domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, flow and timing.
We evaluated all four domainsfor riskof bias, andthe first three alsoregarding applicability.
2.5 Diagnostic accuracy measures and synthesis of results
The data extraction from the selected studies was focused on the patients' characteristics, the
type, thenumberand theanatomical positioningofsensorsused. Theaccuracyandreliability
measures of the IMUs compared to the gold standard optoelectronic 3D motion analysis
system and the correlation of the metrics between the two systems were also primary areas
of interest.

--- PAGE 17 ---
8
3. RESULTS
The initial search retrieved 279 publications. After removing duplicates, remained 157
studies. Through title and abstract reading, we included 35 articles for full-text reading.
Finally, five studies were included in this review.

3.1 Demographic data
A total of 109subjects between 17 and40years oldwere examined. Only one study included
a healthy control group consisting of 17 people. Ninety-two had undergone ACL
reconstruction, with time since surgery ranging from three months to three and a half years.
The majority of the patients had undergone surgery four months ago (Table 3.1).

3.4 Test Tasks
The test procedures to investigate the load differences in ACLR subjects were different
amongst the studies. Patterson et al. (2014) and Sigward et al. (2016) incorporated walking,
Havens et al. (2018) running, and Pratt et al. (2018) a single limb loading task. (Table 3.4)

onto a single limb, lowering themselves as far as they could, and then returned to
the starting position without pausing.

3.5 Risk of bias and applicability concerns
Considering the risk of bias and applicability, we evaluated each article according to the
QUADAS-2 tool. Patient selection in all studies was rated as high risk because there was not
clear how the collection was performed. Pattersonet al. (2014) incorporated a control group,
which could have exaggerated the diagnostic accuracy of the index test.
In the index test and reference standard domains, we rated the risk of bias unclear in all the
studies. The main concern was if the results of the one could have influenced the
interpretation of the other. Flow and timing domain was rated as low risk of bias, but not all
subjects received the same reference standard in three studies. Finally, all studies were rated
as low in terms of the applicability domain.
3.6 IMUs Diagnostic accuracy
In all eligible studies, the use of IMUs revealed significant differences between limbs or
between the ACLR group and control in some metrics. In two studies, inertial sensors were
tested during walking. Patterson et al. (2014) found no differences in temporal parameters
between ACLR and control. Still, they revealed significant differences in three gyroscope
variables, peak shank angular velocity (SAV) at midstance, minimum rotation rate at initial
contact, and post heel strike shank adjustments. All the gyroscope extracted features
significantly differed between the ACLR and the control group and were positively
correlated.

--- PAGE 21 ---
12
On the other hand, Sigward et al. (2016) found no differences between limbs during stance
and swing phase but found differences at peak SAV during loading response. The review
included two studies from Pratt et al. (2018). Both of them used inertial sensors during a
dynamic single limb loading task. Metrics were taken during the deceleration phase. The
first one used only two sensors at thighs and found asymmetries at peak thigh angular
velocity (TAV). The second one placed two more sensors at the shanks and revealed
differences between knee angular velocity (KAV), TAV and SAV for the ACLR limbs.
Finally, Havens et al. (2018) used the metrics from the accelerometer but found no
differences between limbs in the thigh and shank axial acceleration during running.

3.7 Motion analysis systems' diagnostic accuracy
Optoelectronic motion analysis systems are the gold standard for revealing asymmetries in
all fivestudies. Pattersonet al. (2014) foundthatthe ACLR groupdisplayed lower peakknee
adduction moments during early stance. Also, the ACLR group showed small knee joint
angular kinematic differences during the swing phase (more extended and adducted knee
position). No temporal or spatial parameter alterations were noted between groups. Sigward
et al. (2016) found differences in peak knee internal extensor moment during loading
response (approximately 20% of stance) but no differences at temporal events of gait. In
their first study, Pratt et al. (2018) calculated net joint power, peak knee power absorption
and knee power symmetry ratios and foundthe last smaller on the ACLR limb. Inthe second
study, Pratt et al. (2018) recorded peak knee extensor moment, knee angular velocity, thigh
angular velocity and shank angular velocity. All features were smaller on the ACLR limb.
Finally, Havenset al.(2018)utilizedpeakverticalGRF, peakkneeextensor moment,sagittal
plane peak knee power absorption, peak knee joint angular velocity and knee range of
motion. Compared to the non-surgical limb, individuals exhibited smaller knee joint
biomechanical variables.

Sagittal plane knee range of motion

--- PAGE 23 ---
14
3.8 IMUs correlation with the Motion analysis system
All eligible studies integrated motion analysis systems into their experiments along with
IMUs. In Patterson et al. (2014) study, the ACLR participants displayed significantly lower
peak knee adduction moments at early stance. Still, the results did not confirm a correlation
with the reduced shank rotation rate acquired from the IMUs during the swing phase. The
second article testing walking by Sigward et al. (2016) found a positive correlation between
knee extensor moment (KMom) and shank angular velocity during the loading response
phase. Greater shank angular velocity was related to greater knee extensor moment. In the
first article from Pratt et al. (2018), thigh angular velocity symmetry ratios (peak TAV in
reconstructed limb divided by peak TAV in non-surgical limb) positively correlated with
knee power ratio (knee power absorption in the reconstructed limb divided by knee power
absorption in the non-surgical knee).Inertial sensor measurements showed nofalse positives
(100% specificity) and a few false negatives (81,2% sensitivity). In the second article from
Pratt et al. (2018), the statistical analysis indicated strong agreement between measurements
systems for KAV, TAV, and SAV during single limb loading test (SLL). Furthermore, TAV
was strongly correlated with knee power absorption (KPow) and moderately associated with
knee extensor moment (KMom). Finally, Havens et al. (2018) found that limb differences in
thigh axial acceleration were the only predictor of ground reaction force (GRF) differences
and knee power absorption.
Table 3.7. Summary of correlation between extracted variables of the two systems

4. DISCUSSION
The purpose of this review is to investigate whether the use of IMUs can reliably reveal
loading differences after an ACLR surgery. We included five studies, and a total of 109
participants were analyzed. Angular velocities derived from IMUs were the primary
outcome measure. Two studies (Patterson, 2014; Sigward, 2016) tested these portable
devices during walking and found lower SAV in the ACLR limb than in the healthy
limb or control group. In particular, ACLR limbs depicted differences in SAV during
the swing, initial contact, andloadingresponse. Pratt et al.(2018) presentedtwo articles
with the same SLL task measuring angular velocities during the deceleration phase. In
both of them, SAV and TAV were lower. In one study (Havens et al., 2018), thigh and
shank axial acceleration was the prime variable of interest, but it did not differ during
running.
Regarding theassociation betweenthemetricsfrom IMUsandthegold standardmotion
analysissystem, thigh and shank angular velocitieswerepositivelycorrelatedwith knee
extensor moment and knee power absorption. Pratt et al. (2018) also demonstrated that
thigh angular velocity was more predictive of KPow and KMom than SAV. Lastly,
Havens et al. (2018) correlated thigh axial acceleration with GRF and KPow.
To our knowledge, thisis thefirst review focusingon the use of IMUs in assessing knee
function after ACLR surgery compared with gold standard motion analysis systems.
Petraglia et al. (2019) recently reviewed the application of IMUs versus traditional
methods in gait analysis, but the included studies did not have any participants with
orthopedic knee conditions.
Another scoping review was issued in 2019 by Small et al. investigating wearable
sensors' methodology and clinical application to evaluate patient recovery and
functional outcomes following knee arthroplasty. This work provides a comprehensive
image of the aforementioned aspects without a detailed comparison with the motion
analysis systems.

--- PAGE 25 ---
16
4.1 Clinical implications and considerations
Throughout the literature, researchers use IMUs to identify movement disorders across
a broad spectrum of neurological and orthopaedical conditions. They have shown good
agreement with classical gait analysis systems regarding the spatio-temporal
parameters, even in real-life situations (Petraglia et al., 2019). Gait pattern studies have
shown that the kinematics in the sagittal plane of the reconstructed limb return to the
normal level of healthy subjects after six months (Gao, 2010; Leporace, 2012). Spatio-
temporal variables are not suitable parameters to distinguish knee gait biomechanics of
ACLR subjectsfrom healthy onesandshould not beusedasbenchmarksin determining
return to sports after ACL reconstruction (Leporace et al., 2016).
Throughout the rehabilitation process, ACLR results in subtle and persistent kinematic
and kinetic alterations in the knee and consequently in lower extremity movement
patterns. These changes may not be detrimental for the ACL craft while walking, but
they have been associated with the early onset of knee osteoarthritis (Gokeler, 2013;
Slater, 2017).
In this review, two studies have confirmed that direct outputs from IMUs can reveal
differences in shank angular velocities during walking even in individuals three years
post-ACLR. Furthermore, Sigward et al. (2016) established a link between the
kinematic differences detected with the IMUs and loading impairments assessed with
the motion analysis system. Specifically, the lowershank angular velocity of theACLR
limb is correlated with the lower knee extensor moment. During the second rocker of
gait, the tibia is rolled forward over the talus, rotating around the ankle joint (Mayich
et al., 2014). At that point, the shank rotates faster than the femur, resulting in knee
flexion, which coincides with a peak knee extensor moment generated by the activation
of the quadriceps. The recovery of quadriceps strength is often incomplete even years
after surgery (Krishnan et al., 2011). Detecting between limp differences in shank
angular velocity during loading response with the help of IMUs may be helpful for the
clinician to assess between limp deficits and address them in their everyday practice.

--- PAGE 26 ---
17
The most significant hurdle for sports clinicians is how to return the athlete to their
original sport or anyindividual whohas undergonean ACLR surgery at an even greater
level of functional ability and, at the same time, significantly reducing the possibility
of reinjury (Kaplan et al., 2019). Eighty-one percent of individuals return to some form
of sport after surgery, 65% return to their previous level of sport, and 55% return to
competitive sport (Ardern, 2014; Lai, 2018). Nevertheless, even after rehabilitation,
between 35% and 45% of injured athletes will not return to perform at premorbid levels
(Sepulveda et al., 2017). Moreover, there is an increased reinjury rate among young
athletes who haveundergoneanACLR; 1 in 4sustain another ACL injury at some point
in their career relatively early upon their return to high-risk sport (Wiggins, 2014;
Paterno, 2014). Presently, there is still no gold standard to clear athletes for return to
sport (RTS) after ACLR surgery. The clinical decision is multifactorial and based on a
combination of physical and psychological factors (Cheney et al., 2020).
The evidence from thetwo studies from Pratt et al. (2018) suggests that IMUs can serve
as a valuable tool to detect dynamic loading deficits of the knee when the patient is
ready for a more challenging task like running. A previous study from Dowling et al.
(2012) has reported a relationship between coronal plane thigh and shank angular
velocities and knee adductor moments in a healthy population during a jump landing
task. Pratt et al. (2018) correlated segment angular velocity to joint power (product of
joint moment and jointangular velocity), exploringthepower absorptionduring sagittal
plane loading. These results imply that in the lack of force platforms and a marker-
based motion capture system, inertial sensors and, more specifically, a sensor based on
the thigh may be helpful in the clinic to quantify modified knee loading during a single
limb loading task after an ACLR surgery.
At this point, two more studies can be mentioned even though they were not met the
inclusion criteria. The first is from Setuain et al. (2015), which quantifies jumping
biomechanics using direct mechanics-based approaches to simplify the measurement
methodology. They studied the behavior of the center of mass during various jumping
activities, taking into consideration the complete body as a single system of mass and
inertia. For that reason, a single IMU was used in the L3 area where the human's center
of gravity is thought to be. After identifying the various events of the jumping task
(based on vertical velocity records), the linear acceleration, direction, and jumping

--- PAGE 27 ---
18
phase timings were assessed to determine the important parameters for each phase.
Compared to their non-ACL injured counterparts, ACL-reconstructed athletes had
higher supporting three-axis peak accelerations and worse jumping performance
(expressed as the duration in seconds of the flight time phase of the jump).
The second one is from Dan et al. (2019). They predicted changes in limb kinetics
during functionalexercisethatthecurrent returntosportsassessmentsdoesnot identify.
The current study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of this accelerometer,
gyroscope system, and pressure sensor mat in detecting patients' kinetic differences
prior to returning to sport after ACL surgery. The main factors of concern were varus
and valgus alignment. ACL patients showed more significant deviations in the
reconstructed leg when undertakingsingle-leg exercises such as the single-leg box drop
and single-leg squat. There were no variations in alignment in the double leg activities;
however, the force plate revealed that the reconstructed leg involves less force than the
contralateral leg.Theforceplatealsodemonstratedareducedflyingtimeintherepaired
leg during a single-leg hop test. IMUs did not find any asymmetrical variations in
coronal alignment in double-leg exercise. This might be explained by the patient
adjusting to accept less force through the repaired limb, but the force plate detects less
force via the repaired leg in a double leg landing.
Inertial-based motion capture handles many limitations of traditional motion capture
systems, such as marker occlusion, expensive equipment costs, and performing
movements in a confined laboratory environment. The accuracy of IMU systems is
mainly determined by the data fusion algorithms and pose estimation methodologies
used to interpret human motion from raw IMU data. Also, there are several sources of
possible error. To enhance IMU-derived spatiotemporal and kinematic estimations, the
clinician must consider the effect of soft tissue artifacts, device placement,
biomechanical modeling methods, and ferromagnetic interference within the
environment. (Hindle et al., 2021).
4.2 Limitations
Thecurrent study hasanumber of limitations.Firstof all, althoughweretrievedenough
articles referring to the dynamic assessment of the knee after an ACLR surgery with
the use of IMUs, only five met the eligible criteria. Most of the studies excluded from

--- PAGE 28 ---
19
this review lacked a concurrent evaluation by a gold standard optoelectronic system or
did not incorporate an ACLR population. Secondly, the included studies were not
uniform regarding the executed tasks and the outcome measures. Precisely, we
encountered three different tasks that the authors used to compare knee function and
various outcome measures. Additionally, it is unknown if the reported diagnostic
accuracy applies to other phases of rehabilitation than those mentioned or is maintained
with multiple dynamic tests. Future studies are needed to establish a more standardized
test procedure and incorporate IMUs as a diagnostic tool.
4.3 Conclusion
Inertial sensor measurement units can serve as a valuable instrument in the clinical
quantification of dynamickneeloadingasymmetries. Intheabsenceof high-endmotion
analysis systems and force platforms, inertial sensors may be a practical alternative for
analyzing knee function. Further development is needed to improve their techniques
and their application in an ACLR population

Στόχος: Ο πρωταρχικός σκοπός αυτού του άρθρου είναι η συστηματική ανασκόπηση
της βιβλιογραφίας σχετικά με το εάν οι φορητοί και οικονομικά προσιτoί αδρανειακοί
αισθητήρες, μπορούν να αποκαλύψουν με αξιοπιστία κινηματικές ασυμμετρίες μεταξύ
των άκρων σε ασθενείς με ανακατασκευή Πρόσθιου Χιαστού Συνδέσμου (ΠΧΣ).
Σχεδιασμός: Συστηματική ανασκόπηση σύμφωνα με τις οδηγίες PRISMA-DTA
Μεθοδολογία: Πραγματοποιήσαμε συστηματική αναζήτηση στη βάσηδεδομένων των
PUBMED, CINAHL, SCOPUS καιSPORTDISCUS, ελέγχοντας γιαδημοσιεύσεις που
συνέκριναν τη χρήση αδρανειακών αισθητήρων με οπτοηλεκτρονικά συστήματα
ανάλυσης κίνησης, αξιολογώντας άτομα με ανακατασκευασμένο (ΠΧΣ) κατά τη
διάρκεια μιας δυναμικής δοκιμής ή περπατήματος. Κάθε επιλέξιμη μελέτη
αξιολογήθηκε για τη μεθοδολογική της ποιότητα σύμφωνα με τη λίστα ελέγχου
QUADAS-2
Αποτελέσματα: Αρχικά ανακτήθηκαν 279 άρθρα και τελικά πέντε πληρούσαν τα
κριτήρια συμπερίληψης στην έρευνα. Τα εξαγόμενα χαρακτηριστικά από
αδρανειακούς αισθητήρες αποκάλυψαν σημαντικές διαφορές μεταξύ των άκρων σε
ασθενείς με ανακατασκευασμένο (ΠΧΣ) σε τέσσερις μελέτες. Ορισμένα από αυτά τα
χαρακτηριστικά συσχετίστηκαν ισχυρά με μετρήσεις που αποκτήθηκαν από τα
συστήματα ανάλυσης κίνησης.
Συμπέρασμα: Οι αδρανειακοί αισθητήρες μπορούν να παρέχουν συγκρίσιμες
πληροφορίες με τα συστήματα ανάλυσης κίνησης κατά τη δυναμική αξιολόγηση του
γόνατος μετά από χειρουργική επέμβαση (ΠΧΣ). Αυτό έχει σημαντικές δυνατότητες
για κλινική χρήση, ενισχύοντας τη λειτουργική αξιολόγηση των ασθενών και την
παρακολούθηση της διαδικασίας αποκατάστασης τους.
Λέξεις κλειδιά: αδρανειακοί αισθητήρες, αξιολόγηση γόνατος, πρόσθιος χιαστός,
διαγνωστική ακρίβεια.
